text.little: Your heart goes thump, thump, all day long!
text.young: Your heart beats about 100,000 times every day.
text.junior: Your heart pumps about 7,000 litres of blood every day, enough to fill dozens of bathtubs.

text.young: Your thigh bone is the longest bone in your body.
text.junior: The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body, about a quarter of your height.

text.little: Your ears have teeny tiny bones inside!
text.young: The smallest bone in your body is inside your ear.
text.junior: The stapes in the middle ear is the smallest bone in the body, only about 3 mm long.

text.young: Babies have more bones than grown-ups! Some join together as you grow.
text.junior: Babies are born with around 300 bones; many fuse as they grow, leaving about 206 in adults.

text.little: Your skin covers you from head to toe!
text.young: Your skin is your body's biggest organ.
text.junior: Skin is the largest organ, and its whole outer layer is replaced about once a month.

text.little: Blink, blink! Your eyes blink to stay clean.
text.young: You blink many times every minute to keep your eyes clean and wet.
text.junior: Most people blink around 15–20 times a minute, which spreads tears across the eye.

text.young: Your small intestine is longer than a car!
text.junior: The small intestine is about 6 metres long, but it fits neatly coiled up in your abdomen.

text.young: Your brain keeps working even while you sleep.
text.junior: Your brain has about 86 billion neurons, all sending messages to each other.

text.young: Some nerve messages zoom faster than a racing car!
text.junior: The fastest nerve signals travel at over 100 metres per second.

text.young: Your left lung is a little smaller to make room for your heart.
text.junior: Spread out flat, the inner surface of your lungs would cover about half a tennis court.

text.young: Your kidneys clean your blood all day and night.
text.junior: Your kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid a day, but only about 1.5 litres leaves the body as urine.

text.young: Your stomach can stretch to hold a big meal!
text.junior: The stomach lining makes a layer of mucus so its strong acid doesn't digest the stomach itself.

text.young: You have more than 600 muscles!
text.junior: The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle, and the sartorius is the longest.

text.young: Blood goes all around your body again and again.
text.junior: A red blood cell lives for about 120 days before it is recycled.

text.young: Your blood vessels are so long they could wrap around the Earth!
text.junior: Laid end to end, your blood vessels would stretch about 100,000 km, more than twice around the Earth.

text.young: Your hair grows a little bit every day.
text.junior: Head hair grows about 1 cm a month.

text.little: Wiggle your fingers! Your fingernails keep growing.
text.young: Your fingernails grow faster than your toenails.
text.junior: Fingernails grow several times faster than toenails.

text.young: Hiccups happen when your diaphragm makes a sudden jump.
text.junior: Hiccups are sudden, involuntary contractions of the diaphragm.

text.young: You are a tiny bit taller in the morning than at bedtime!
text.junior: The discs in your spine squash slightly during the day, so you can be about 1 cm taller in the morning.

text.young: Babies' kneecaps are soft and turn into bone as they grow.
text.junior: The patella begins as cartilage and hardens into bone during early childhood.

text.young: The front of your eye is clear, like a window.
text.junior: The cornea has no blood vessels; it gets much of its oxygen straight from the air.

text.young: Your liver can regrow parts of itself!
text.junior: The liver can regrow to its full size even after part of it has been removed.

text.little: Ah-choo! Sneezes blow dust out of your nose.
text.young: Your eyes close by themselves every time you sneeze.
text.junior: Closing the eyes during a sneeze is an automatic reflex.

text.young: Goosebumps happen when tiny muscles pull your hairs up.
text.junior: Goosebumps are caused by tiny arrector pili muscles attached to hair follicles.

text.little: Grumble, rumble! Your tummy makes noises.
text.young: Tummy rumbles are made by food, gas and juices moving through your gut.
text.junior: The rumbling sound of the gut has a scientific name: borborygmi.

text.young: You are made of trillions of tiny cells!
text.junior: The human body is made of about 37 trillion cells.

text.young: Your biggest muscle is in your bottom!
text.junior: The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the body; it helps you stand up and climb.

text.young: Your 'funny bone' isn't really a bone!
text.junior: The 'funny bone' tingle comes from the ulnar nerve being bumped at the elbow.

text.little: Stick out your tongue! It helps you taste yummy food.
text.young: Your tongue can taste sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savoury.
text.junior: Taste buds all over the tongue can detect all five tastes; the old 'tongue map' is a myth.

text.young: Your spinal cord helps you pull your hand away from something hot, super fast!
text.junior: Reflexes like pulling away from heat are handled by the spinal cord before the brain even notices.
